steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our CHI-style paper on whether user characteristics (age, gender, experience, personality) matter for how people engage with, understand and trust AI explanations. Motivate XAI, summarize prior evidence on user characteristics, state our research questions and contributions, and end with what the results imply for personalized XAI.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. AI is ubiquitous; need for XAI (transparency, trust)
2. XAI methods: global and local explanations, mental models
3. Evidence that user characteristics affect how explanations are received
4. Gap and our study; four research questions
5. Contributions and implication for personalized XAI

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. AI ubiquity and need for XAI
- AI applications increasingly ubiquitous: spam emails, loan eligibility, generating language
- rapid advances, seamless integration into people's lives -> XAI critical for transparency and trust
- repercussions of automated decisions; increasing regulatory oversight

2. XAI methods
- global and local explanations
- global: overview of model functioning; local: how specific predictions generated for individual instances
- help end users build accurate mental models -> understanding and trust
- 'opening up' black-box inner workings

3. User characteristics
- growing evidence that user characteristics affect how explanations are received
- characteristics: age, gender, personality, experience (not limited to)
- other fields: personality in recommender systems, Human-Robot Interaction
- information retrieval: previous experience impacts search behavior
- XAI: gender + educational background affect preferred explanation types and trust
- personality traits impact interaction with explanations
- impetus for personalizing XAI, tailoring design/presentation of explanations

4. Gap + study
- understanding still limited
- test whether user characteristics associated with engagement, understanding, trust
- interactive AI system with local explanations for flagging inappropriate comments
- RQ1 engagement in finding misclassifications; RQ2 perceived understanding; RQ3 actual understanding; RQ4 trust

5. Contributions
- prototype with local explanations for flagging inappropriate comments (section 3.1), open-source; guides participants, logs interactions; Detoxify multi-class classifier; explanations per comment; participants gave feedback
- methodology: large-scale study, 149 participants from Prolific (section 3.3); age, gender, previous experience, Big 5 traits vs engagement, trust, perceived and actual understanding
- evidence: very few characteristics related to outcomes; only age and openness associated with actual understanding (section 4)
- argue to reorient user-focused XAI research pursuing personalized XAI based on fine-grained user characteristics (section 5)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are becoming more and more ubiquitous, from identifying spam emails to deciding who is eligible for loans to generating language. Because AI is advancing so quickly and is being integrated seamlessly into people's lives, the need for Explainable AI (XAI) has become critical for fostering transparency and trust. This need for transparency and trust is very clear, not least because automated decisions can have repercussions on people's lives and because there is more and more regulatory oversight of AI systems.

To respond to this need, the XAI field has made a lot of progress in developing methods for giving explanations, for example global and local explanations for AI models. Global explanations give an overview of how the model works, while local explanations go into how specific predictions were generated for individual instances. Explanations in AI systems can help end users build accurate mental models of the AI systems, which improves both their understanding and how much they trust these systems. These methods have improved users' comprehension of AI systems by 'opening up' how their black-box inner workings work.

At the same time, there is more and more evidence that the characteristics of a user may affect how explanations are received. User characteristics usually include a broad range of attributes, like age, gender, personality, and experience, among others. The influence of user characteristics has been studied in other fields too, for example personality has been studied a lot in recommender systems and in Human-Robot Interaction. Information retrieval research has shown that previous experience affects search behavior. Specifically in XAI, gender and educational background were found to affect what types of explanations participants preferred and also their trust. Personality traits were found to impact how people interact with explanations. This has given some impetus to work that tries to use the characteristics of users to personalize XAI and to tailor how explanations are designed and presented to users.

4. Gap + study (to write up)
- understanding still limited -> test whether user characteristics associated with engagement, understanding, trust
- interactive AI system, local explanations for flagging inappropriate comments
- RQ1: engagement in finding misclassifications
- RQ2: perceived understanding of explanations
- RQ3: actual understanding of explanations
- RQ4: degree of trust in AI system

5. Contributions (to write up)
- prototype, local explanations, flagging inappropriate comments (section 3.1); open-source; guides study, logs interactions; Detoxify classifier; explanations per comment; participant feedback
- methodology: large-scale study, 149 Prolific participants (section 3.3); age, gender, previous experience, Big 5 vs engagement, trust, perceived/actual understanding
- very few characteristics related to outcomes; only age and openness -> actual understanding (section 4)
- reorient user-focused XAI research on personalized XAI based on fine-grained characteristics (section 5)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are becoming more and more ubiquitous, from identifying spam emails to deciding who is eligible for loans to generating language. Because AI is advancing so quickly and is being integrated seamlessly into people's lives, the need for Explainable AI (XAI) has become critical for fostering transparency and trust. This need for transparency and trust is very clear, not least because automated decisions can have repercussions on people's lives and because there is more and more regulatory oversight of AI systems.

To respond to this need, the XAI field has made a lot of progress in developing methods for giving explanations, for example global and local explanations for AI models. Global explanations give an overview of how the model works, while local explanations go into how specific predictions were generated for individual instances. Explanations in AI systems can help end users build accurate mental models of the AI systems, which improves both their understanding and how much they trust these systems. These methods have improved users' comprehension of AI systems by 'opening up' how their black-box inner workings work.

At the same time, there is more and more evidence that the characteristics of a user may affect how explanations are received. User characteristics usually include a broad range of attributes, like age, gender, personality, and experience, among others. The influence of user characteristics has been studied in other fields too, for example personality has been studied a lot in recommender systems and in Human-Robot Interaction. Information retrieval research has shown that previous experience affects search behavior. Specifically in XAI, gender and educational background were found to affect what types of explanations participants preferred and also their trust. Personality traits were found to impact how people interact with explanations. This has given some impetus to work that tries to use the characteristics of users to personalize XAI and to tailor how explanations are designed and presented to users.

These works give some evidence that there might be a link between user characteristics and AI explanations, but our understanding is still limited. So we set out to test if user characteristics are associated with how users engage with explanations, how well they understand these explanations, and how much trust users give to AI systems. To do this, we developed an interactive AI system that gives local explanations for flagging inappropriate comments, and we came up with four Research Questions (RQs):

- RQ1: How do user characteristics relate to user engagement in finding misclassifications?

- RQ2: How do user characteristics relate to the perceived understanding of explanations?

- RQ3: How do user characteristics relate to the actual understanding of explanations?

- RQ4: How do user characteristics relate to the degree of trust users attribute to an AI system?

By answering these questions, we make three main contributions:

- • We provide a prototype that gives local explanations in the task of flagging inappropriate comments (section 3.1), and we release it open-source. The prototype guides participants through the user study and logs what users do. We used an existing multi-class classifier called Detoxify with the prototype, and we generated explanations for each comment. Participants interacted with the explanations given in the prototype and gave feedback on them.

- • We advance the methodology for investigating user characteristics in XAI. We ran a large-scale study with 149 participants recruited from Prolific (section 3.3). We used the prototype to investigate what effect users' characteristics, specifically age, gender, previous experience, and the Big 5 personality traits, have on outcome measures like participants' engagement, trust, and perceived and actual understanding of the XAI system.

- • We show empirical evidence that very few user characteristics are related to our outcome measures of engagement, trust, and understanding. Only age and the personality trait openness were associated with actual understanding (section 4).

Based on these results, we argue that user-focused XAI research that pursues personalized XAI based on fine-grained user characteristics should be reoriented (section 5).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly ubiquitous [1], from identifying spam emails to determining eligibility for loans to generating language. With the rapid advancement of AI and its seamless integration into people's lives, the need for Explainable AI (XAI) has become critical to foster transparency and trust [2]. This need is more than evident, not least because of the potential repercussions of automated decisions on people's lives and the increasing regulatory oversight of AI systems [3,4,5].

In response, the field of XAI has made substantial progress in developing methods for providing explanations, such as global and local explanations for AI models [6,7]. Global explanations offer an overview of the model's functioning, whereas local explanations delve into how specific predictions were generated for individual instances. Explanations can assist end users in constructing accurate mental models of AI systems, thereby enhancing both their understanding and the degree of trust they attribute to these systems [8,9]. These methods have improved users' comprehension of AI systems by 'opening up' their black-box inner workings [2].

At the same time, there is growing evidence that a user's characteristics may have an impact on how explanations are received [10,11,12]. User characteristics typically span a broad range of attributes, including but not limited to age, gender, personality, and experience. Their influence has been studied in other fields; for example, personality has been extensively studied in the context of recommender systems [13,14,15] and Human-Robot Interaction [16,17], and information retrieval research has revealed that previous experience impacts search behavior [18,19,20,21,22]. Specific to XAI, gender and educational background have been found to affect both the types of explanations participants preferred and their trust [23], and personality traits have been found to impact the interaction with explanations [24,25]. This has provided some impetus to work that aims to use users' characteristics to personalize XAI and tailor the design and presentation of explanations to users [26].

While these works provide some evidence of a potential link between user characteristics and AI explanations, our understanding remains limited. We therefore set out to test whether user characteristics are associated with user engagement with explanations, the understanding of these explanations, and the degree of trust users attribute to AI systems. To do so, we developed an interactive AI system that provides local explanations for flagging inappropriate comments, and formulated four Research Questions (RQs):

- RQ1: How do user characteristics relate to user engagement in finding misclassifications?

- RQ2: How do user characteristics relate to the perceived understanding of explanations?

- RQ3: How do user characteristics relate to the actual understanding of explanations?

- RQ4: How do user characteristics relate to the degree of trust users attribute to an AI system?

In addressing these questions, we make three main contributions:

- • We provide a prototype that provides local explanations in the task of flagging inappropriate comments (section 3.1), which we release open-source. The prototype guides participants through the user study and logs their interactions. We used a pre-existing multi-class classifier named Detoxify [27] with our prototype and generated explanations for each comment. Participants interacted with and provided feedback on the explanations using the prototype.

- • We advance the methodology of investigating user characteristics in XAI. We conducted a large-scale study with 149 participants recruited from Prolific (section 3.3), using our prototype to investigate the effect of users' characteristics, specifically age, gender, previous experience, and the Big 5 personality traits, on outcome measures such as participants' engagement, trust, and perceived and actual understanding of the XAI system.

- • We show empirical evidence that very few user characteristics are related to our outcome measures of engagement, trust, and understanding. Only age and the personality trait openness were associated with actual understanding (section 4).

In light of these results, we argue for reorienting user-focused XAI research that pursues personalized XAI based on fine-grained user characteristics (section 5).
